section_summary: This section documents U.S. diplomatic and congressional efforts to help the Jewish Tigner family leave Soviet-controlled Lviv by obtaining Japanese transit visas, Soviet exit permission, and onward admission to a Western Hemisphere country. The correspondence traces requests from the family’s relatives Samuel and Harold Cline through Senator William H. King to the State Department and the U.S. Embassy in Moscow. By June 19, Sofia Tigner and her sons Jerzy and Marek were traveling through Vladivostok to Tokyo, while Aron Tigner remained behind awaiting a Soviet exit visa; the section ends with administrative index and cross-reference sheets.

subfiles.title: Closing page of letter from Sumner Welles concerning the Cline–Tigner case
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Welles forwards the Moscow Embassy’s suggestions concerning assistance to Samuel and Harold Cline in the Tigner case.
subfiles.summary: Only the closing portion of the letter appears in this section. Welles refers the Moscow Embassy’s suggestions concerning Samuel and Harold Cline to the recipient’s attention and lists the Embassy’s June 7 telegram as an enclosure.

subfiles.title: Telegram 641 from Moscow concerning alternate routes for the Tigner family
subfiles.about: The Embassy proposes Mediterranean or trans-Pacific travel arrangements for the Tigners and requests authority to consider temporary visitor visas.
subfiles.summary: Collins was attempting to secure Mexican visas, but Polish and stateless Jews could not obtain Italian transit visas. The Embassy suggested either passage from Istanbul or another non-Italian Mediterranean port, or travel through Vladivostok, Japan, and the United States if entry into Mexico or another American republic could be arranged. The Japanese Embassy had been instructed to assist, and the U.S. Embassy requested authorization to accept temporary-visitor-visa applications.

subfiles.title: Telegram 634 from Moscow on obstacles to the Tigners’ departure
subfiles.about: The Embassy explains the incomplete financial, passport, destination-visa, and Soviet exit arrangements preventing the Tigner family’s journey.
subfiles.summary: The Tigners had asked Jack Collins to obtain entry visas to an American republic, purchase transportation from Genoa onward, and remit $400 for expenses, but he had not done so. They lacked passports and instead had travel affidavits executed before Ward in Lviv. Japanese officials doubted that visas could be issued on those affidavits without destination-country residence visas, while Soviet authorities would not issue exit visas without admission to a neighboring country or the first port of call. The Embassy therefore believed arrangements through Collins might be more practical than the Japanese route.

subfiles.title: Department telegram 308 directing assistance for Aron David Tigner
subfiles.about: The Department directs the Embassy to assist Aron David Tigner and his family following Senator King’s intervention.
subfiles.summary: Senator King reported that Aron David Tigner, his wife Sofia, and their children Jerzy and Marek were Polish citizens living in Lviv. He understood that they possessed Soviet departure papers and Japanese visas expiring June 5. After the Japanese Embassy in Washington promised to contact its Moscow embassy, the Department instructed the U.S. Embassy to do what it could if the family approached it.

subfiles.title: Letter from Sumner Welles to Senator King acknowledging action
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Welles informs King that the Embassy in Moscow has been instructed to help the Tigner family travel through Japan.
subfiles.summary: Welles acknowledges King’s June 4 request for assistance to Aron David Tigner and his family. He states that the Department telegraphed the Embassy in Moscow with the pertinent facts and asked it to facilitate the family’s journey as far as appropriately possible.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s memorandum ordering action on Senator King’s request
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Welles instructs Hamilton to ask the Moscow Embassy to facilitate the Tigners’ trip to Japan and to prepare a reply to Senator King.
subfiles.summary: Welles characterizes the matter as a personal request from Senator King. He directs Hamilton to send the Embassy in Moscow the circumstances and ask the chargé to do what is possible to facilitate the family’s travel to Japan. Hamilton is also to draft a reply for Welles’s signature.

subfiles.title: Letter from Senator King requesting extension of the Tigners’ Japanese visas
subfiles.about: King asks the State Department to help extend Japanese visas for Aron and Sofia Tigner and their children.
subfiles.summary: King relays a request from Utah lawyers Samuel and Harold Cline concerning their relatives Aron and Sofia Tigner and the children Jerzy and Marek. The family reportedly had Soviet departure papers and Japanese visas, but the visas expired on June 5 before travel arrangements could be completed. King asks the Department to have the American representative in Moscow approach Japanese officials for a reasonable extension.

subfiles.title: Letter from Senator King to Julian Harrington
subfiles.to: Julian Harrington, Visa Division, State Department
subfiles.about: King requests prompt State Department intervention to extend the Tigner family’s Japanese visas.
subfiles.summary: King explains that Samuel and Harold Cline had relatives in Lviv who possessed papers to leave Russia and visas to enter Japan. Because the visas expired June 5, he asks Harrington to arrange contact between the American consul in Moscow and the appropriate Russian and Japanese authorities. He emphasizes the Clines’ credibility, encloses their telegram, and requests prompt attention.

subfiles.title: Western Union telegram from Samuel and Harold Cline to Senator King
subfiles.from: Samuel and Harold Cline, Milford, Utah
subfiles.to: Senator William H. King, Washington, D.C.
subfiles.about: The Clines urgently ask King to secure diplomatic help for their Tigner relatives’ departure from Russia through Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Clines identify Aron and Sofia Tigner and their children Jerzy and Marek at an address in Lviv and stress that their Japanese visas would expire June 5. They ask the State Department to contact American and Japanese officials in Moscow and Tokyo, guaranteeing financial support for the family. Their immediate priority is to get the family out of Russia, with later travel to the United States or another Western Hemisphere country. They offer to pay cable and contact expenses and ask King to notify them if messages are sent.

subfiles.title: Telegram 704 reporting Sofia Tigner and her sons en route to Japan
subfiles.about: The Embassy reports that Sofia Tigner and her sons have left for Japan while Aron Tigner awaits a Soviet exit visa.
subfiles.summary: Sofia Tigner and her sons Jerzy and Marek received Japanese transit visas and departed Moscow by train for Vladivostok. They were expected to reach Tokyo around July 8 and could be contacted through the American Consulate General. Aron Tigner was to follow once he obtained a Soviet exit visa.

subfiles.title: Letter from A. M. Warren concerning the Embassy’s inability to locate Aron D. Tigner
subfiles.from: A. M. Warren, Chief, Visa Division
subfiles.about: Warren reports that the Moscow Embassy has been unable to obtain information about Aron D. Tigner’s whereabouts or plans.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy sent a registered letter to Tigner asking about his whereabouts, welfare, plans, and whether he wanted documents—including an apparent Philippine visa—forwarded to him. Tigner did not reply, and the Embassy could not determine whether he received the letter. Warren states that the Department will inform King of later developments.
